Option D takes the second route — 'Because the application was incomplete' states outright what was lacking, and the main clause then reports what the evaluator did. Meaning and grammar line up with no ambiguity left.

distractorExplanations.A: The modifier now sits correctly beside 'the application,' but the main clause has been reversed: an application cannot return an evaluator. Fixing the dangler broke the sense.
distractorExplanations.B: Moving the phrase into the middle does not change what it modifies. Placed right after 'the evaluator,' it states even more plainly that the evaluator was incomplete.
distractorExplanations.C: 'Incomplete' still dangles onto the evaluator, and the trailing 'by it' has no clear antecedent. The passive construction adds obscurity without repairing the modifier.

tip.label: Grammar Rule
tip.text: After an opening -ing or -ed phrase, the very next noun must be the doer. If it is not, either swap in the right subject or expand the phrase into a because/when clause.

reference: Dangling Modifiers: an introductory participial phrase must modify the subject that follows it

subject: Verbal Ability
question:
Arrange the sentences into the most logical paragraph.

(1) Finally, the validated records are archived.
(2) First, the receiving clerk checks whether the form is complete.
(3) The evaluator then verifies the supporting documents.
(4) After approval, the result is released to the applicant.
explanation: This paragraph describes a procedure, and procedures are ordered by their signal words rather than by guesswork. Four markers do all the work here: 'First' can only open, 'then' must follow something already mentioned, 'After approval' presupposes that an evaluation has already taken place, and 'Finally' must close. Chain them and the office workflow appears in its natural order — receive, verify, release, archive. The reliable habit for sequence items is to lock the first and last sentences using their markers, since that alone usually eliminates three of the four options before you examine the middle.
steps: Step 1 — Anchor the opening. Sentence 2 begins with 'First,' the strongest opening marker in the set, and it also describes the earliest physical event: the clerk receiving the form.
Step 2 — Anchor the closing. Sentence 1 begins with 'Finally' and describes archiving, an action that can only happen once everything else is done.
Step 3 — Place the continuation. Sentence 3 contains 'then,' which requires a preceding step, and verifying supporting documents logically follows the completeness check in sentence 2.
Step 4 — Place the dependent step. Sentence 4 opens with 'After approval,' so it must come after the evaluation in sentence 3 and before the archiving in sentence 1.
Step 5 — Read the assembled order: 2-3-4-1 — receive, verify, release, archive.

distractorExplanations.B: Putting sentence 1 first opens the paragraph with 'Finally,' a word that announces an ending. Archiving records before any of them have been checked also reverses the workflow.
distractorExplanations.C: This order releases the result to the applicant (sentence 4) before the evaluator has verified the documents (sentence 3), so approval would precede the evaluation it depends on.
distractorExplanations.D: Beginning with 'then' in sentence 3 leaves the reader with no prior step to connect it to, and archiving in sentence 1 is placed before the release in sentence 4.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Lock the ends first. 'First, To begin, Initially' can only open; 'Finally, Lastly, In conclusion' can only close. Fixing those two positions usually eliminates most options at once.

subject: Verbal Ability
question: Which sentence should come FIRST in a paragraph explaining disaster preparation?

choices.text: Families should also store water and medicine.
After every drill, officials should evaluate the response.
Preparation begins with identifying the hazards that may affect the community.
Finally, residents should review what they learned.

explanation: A topic sentence has two identifying features: it points forward rather than backward, and it covers the widest ground. Test each candidate for backward-pointing signals — 'also' adds to something already said, 'After every drill' assumes a drill has been described, and 'Finally' closes a list that must already exist. Only option C stands on its own with no unstated antecedent, and it names the general starting point, hazard identification, under which the specific measures in the other sentences would fall. Any sentence that cannot be understood without knowing what came before it is, by definition, not the opener.
steps: Step 1 — Scan for backward-pointing signals. Option A carries 'also,' which can only add to a point already made.
Step 2 — Continue the scan. Option B opens with 'After every drill,' presupposing that drills have already been introduced, and option D opens with 'Finally,' which marks a closing item.
Step 3 — Check what remains. Option C contains no such signal and needs no earlier sentence to make sense.
Step 4 — Confirm by scope. Hazard identification is a general first stage; storing supplies, running drills, and reviewing lessons are specific actions that fit beneath it.
Step 5 — Option C is therefore the topic sentence.

distractorExplanations.A: The word 'also' is a linking signal that requires a preceding recommendation. Opening a paragraph with an addition leaves the reader searching for the point being added to.
distractorExplanations.B: Evaluating a response 'after every drill' assumes drills have already been established as part of the plan, and it describes a late-stage review rather than a starting point.
distractorExplanations.D: 'Finally' explicitly labels the sentence as the last item in a sequence. It also narrows to one closing action, which is the opposite of what a topic sentence must do.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: A topic sentence never leans on an earlier one. Strike out any candidate containing also, however, therefore, this, finally, or a backward time cue — the survivor is your opener.

subject: Verbal Ability
question:
Which sentence does NOT belong in the paragraph?

(1) Digital records can speed up retrieval.
(2) Access controls can protect confidential files.
(3) Regular backups reduce the risk of permanent loss.
(4) The cafeteria introduced a new lunch menu.
(5) Staff training helps prevent handling errors.
explanation: Paragraph unity means every sentence advances one controlling idea. State that idea before judging any sentence: here, four of the five describe ways of managing records well — faster retrieval, restricted access, protection against loss, and fewer handling errors. Sentence 4 reports a change in cafeteria food. It is a perfectly good sentence and may even be true of the same office, but sharing a workplace is not the same as sharing a topic. Relevance is judged against the controlling idea, never against whether the statement is accurate or interesting on its own.
steps: Step 1 — Derive the controlling idea from the sentences that agree. Retrieval speed, access control, backups, and training all concern managing records well.
Step 2 — Test sentence 1: faster retrieval is a benefit of good records management. It fits.
Step 3 — Test sentences 2 and 3: access controls and backups both protect records. Both fit.
Step 4 — Test sentence 5: training staff to handle records correctly supports the same idea. It fits.
Step 5 — Test sentence 4: a new lunch menu concerns cafeteria service, not records. It is the sentence that breaks unity.

distractorExplanations.A: Retrieval speed is one of the main reasons offices digitise records at all. Sentence 1 supports the controlling idea directly and belongs in the paragraph.
distractorExplanations.B: Protecting confidential files through access controls is a core records-management concern. Naming a security measure does not make the sentence off-topic.
distractorExplanations.C: Backups guard against permanent loss of records, which is the same subject the surrounding sentences develop. Sentence 3 sits comfortably within the paragraph.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Write the controlling idea in your own words first, then test each sentence against it. A sentence can be true, well written, and about the same office and still break unity.

subject: Verbal Ability
passage: The city opened an online appointment system. Walk-in congestion declined, but some senior citizens struggled to use the platform. The city therefore retained an assisted service desk.
question: What is the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The city completely prohibited walk-in transactions.
The online system failed to reduce congestion.
The city combined digital service with assistance for users who needed it.
The assisted desk replaced the appointment system.

explanation: A main idea has to account for the whole passage, not one sentence of it. Three movements appear here: the city launched an online system, the system worked but left some senior citizens behind, and the city responded by keeping an assisted desk. Option C holds all three together — a digital channel plus human help for those who need it. The other options each seize on one part and distort it. Beware of absolutes such as 'completely,' 'failed,' and 'replaced'; the passage reports a measured adjustment, and a main idea that overstates the text is wrong even when it names the right topic.

distractorExplanations.A: Nothing in the passage bans walk-ins. Congestion 'declined,' which means walk-ins continued at a lower volume, and the assisted desk exists precisely to serve people in person.
distractorExplanations.B: The text states plainly that walk-in congestion declined, so the system succeeded at its primary purpose. Difficulty for some users is a separate finding, not a failure of the system.
distractorExplanations.D: Both services operate side by side. The desk was 'retained' alongside the appointment system, and retaining something is the opposite of replacing what it supplements.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: A main idea must cover every sentence. If an option ignores part of the passage or hardens it with completely, always, failed, or replaced, it is a distortion rather than a summary.

subject: Verbal Ability
passage: The city opened an online appointment system. Walk-in congestion declined, but some senior citizens struggled to use the platform. The city therefore retained an assisted service desk.
question: Based on the passage, why was the assisted service desk retained?

choices.text: To help people who had difficulty using the online platform

explanation: Detail questions are answered by locating the sentence, not by reasoning about the topic. The word 'therefore' in the final sentence is the pointer: it tells the reader that whatever precedes it is the cause of what follows. What precedes it is that some senior citizens struggled to use the platform; what follows is the decision to retain the assisted desk. Option A restates that cause. Train yourself to treat therefore, thus, so, consequently, and as a result as arrows — the reason is always sitting immediately upstream of them.

distractorExplanations.B: Reducing congestion was the point of the online system, and the passage records that it fell. No agency would keep a service in order to make its own queues longer.
distractorExplanations.C: Cancellation appears nowhere in the text. The desk assists people who cannot use the platform; it does not undo appointments made through it.
distractorExplanations.D: Fees are never mentioned. This option imports a familiar assumption about government transactions rather than anything the passage actually states.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Treat therefore, thus, so, and consequently as arrows pointing backward. For a 'why' question, the reason sits in the clause immediately before the signal word.

subject: Verbal Ability
passage: Public feedback revealed that the original schedule excluded many night-shift workers. The office added Saturday appointments and saw higher participation.
question: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

choices.text: The original schedule was already inclusive.
Adjusting service hours improved access for workers.

explanation: A summary compresses the whole passage to a general level while adding nothing the text does not support. The passage runs a simple chain: a problem is identified through feedback, the office changes its hours, participation rises. Option D captures the chain at one level of abstraction — service hours were adjusted, and access improved. The other three fail on a single test each. Two of them insert absolutes, 'all' and 'always,' that no two-sentence passage could establish, and the third denies the very problem the first sentence reports.

distractorExplanations.A: The workers objected to a schedule that shut them out, not to appointments as such. The blanket word 'all' converts a specific complaint into a sweeping rejection.
distractorExplanations.B: This inverts the outcome and universalises it. Participation rose after Saturday slots were added, and one office's result cannot support a claim about what 'always' happens.
distractorExplanations.C: The opening sentence says the original schedule excluded many night-shift workers, so calling it inclusive contradicts the passage rather than condensing it.

tip.label: Common Mistake
tip.text: Cross out any option containing all, none, always, never, or only unless the passage states it outright. Absolutes are the fastest way to spot an overreaching summary.

subject: Verbal Ability
question: The word MITIGATE in "Trees help mitigate urban heat" most nearly means:
explanation: Mitigate comes from the Latin mitis, meaning mild or gentle, and it means to make something less severe. The object it takes is almost always a harm: mitigate damage, mitigate risk, mitigate the effects of a typhoon. In the sentence, urban heat is the problem and trees are the intervention, so the verb must name a reduction. The word is worth knowing beyond vocabulary items — disaster management documents in the Philippines pair mitigation with preparedness, response, and recovery as the four phases of the cycle, and there it carries this same sense of reducing severity in advance.

distractorExplanations.A: 'Measure' means to quantify. Instruments measure heat; trees act on it. The sentence describes an effect on the temperature, not an assessment of it.
distractorExplanations.B: 'Predict' means to forecast in advance. Nothing about planting trees anticipates future heat, and the sentence reports a present benefit rather than a projection.
distractorExplanations.C: 'Create' points in the opposite direction. Concrete and vehicles create urban heat; the whole reason trees are planted is to counteract what those sources produce.

tip.label: Vocabulary Trick
tip.text: Check the object of the verb. MITIGATE always takes a harm — damage, risk, heat, loss — and always means to soften it. If the object is a benefit, the word is wrong.

subject: Verbal Ability
question: Which statement is an inference from: "All counters were occupied, yet the queue moved steadily because transactions averaged only four minutes"?

choices.text: Fast transactions helped prevent the queue from stalling.

explanation: An inference is a conclusion the text supports without stating it in those words. The sentence supplies a cause with 'because': short four-minute transactions are the reason the queue kept moving despite every counter being busy. Option A puts that relationship in different words, which is exactly what an inference should do. The three rejected options are not weak inferences; they are contradictions. Learn to sort options into three bins — restated by the text, supported but unstated, and denied by the text. Only the middle bin can hold the answer, and anything in the third bin can be eliminated on sight.

distractorExplanations.B: The sentence opens with 'All counters were occupied,' which rules out closures. This option does not go beyond the text; it denies the first clause outright.
distractorExplanations.C: An hour per transaction contradicts the stated average of four minutes, and it would also make the steady movement of the queue impossible.
distractorExplanations.D: A queue that 'moved steadily' is by definition a queue with people in it. Claiming nobody waited erases the very thing the sentence is describing.

tip.label: Logic Rule
tip.text: Sort every option into restates, supports, or contradicts. Inference answers live in the middle bin — new wording, same logic. Anything that fights a stated fact is out immediately.

subject: Verbal Ability
question: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The new policy will ___ how records are classified.
explanation: Two questions settle this item. First, form: the modal 'will' is always followed by a bare infinitive, so any inflected verb is out before meaning is even considered. Second, meaning: the policy influences an existing practice, and the verb for influencing is 'affect.' Honesty about the harder half of the rule pays off here — 'effect' genuinely can be a verb, meaning to bring about or accomplish, as in 'effect change' or 'effect a settlement.' But that sense requires the policy to create classification itself rather than to shape how it is done, which is not what the sentence says.

distractorExplanations.A: 'Effect' as a verb means to bring something into being. Records are already being classified, so the policy shapes an existing practice rather than creating one from nothing.
distractorExplanations.B: The meaning is right but the form is not. A modal such as 'will' takes the bare infinitive, so 'will affects' doubles the tense marking and cannot stand.
distractorExplanations.D: 'Effected' is a past-tense form placed after the future marker 'will,' which is impossible, and it also carries the 'bring about' sense the sentence does not need.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: RAVEN: Remember, Affect is a Verb, Effect is a Noun. Then check the form — after will, can, must, should, always use the bare infinitive.

reference: affect (verb, to influence) vs. effect (noun, a result)

subject: Verbal Ability
question: Choose the sentence with correct subject–verb agreement.

choices.text: Ten kilometers are a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometer is a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometers have been a long distance to walk.
Ten kilometers is a long distance to walk in extreme heat.

explanation: A plural noun does not always mean a plural subject. When a quantity of distance, money, time, or weight is treated as one amount rather than as separate units, it takes a singular verb: ten kilometers is a long walk, five hundred pesos is a fair price, two hours is enough time. The clue is the singular complement — 'a long distance' names one thing, confirming that the subject is being handled as a single measurement. The plural -s stays on 'kilometers' because that is how the unit is written after any number above one; only the verb reflects the singular idea.

distractorExplanations.A: A plural verb splits the ten kilometers into ten separate items. The complement 'a long distance' is singular, which shows the sentence means one continuous stretch.
distractorExplanations.B: Trimming the -s from 'kilometer' is the error here. Any number greater than one takes the plural noun form, even though the verb that follows stays singular.
distractorExplanations.C: Two problems combine: the plural 'have' misreads the measurement as separate units, and the present perfect implies an ongoing state where a simple statement of fact is meant.

tip.label: Grammar Rule
tip.text: One amount, one verb. Distance, money, time, and weight take a singular verb when the total is treated as a single quantity: 'Two hours IS enough,' 'Five hundred pesos IS the fee.'

reference: Subject-Verb Agreement: a measurement treated as a single quantity takes a singular verb

subject: Verbal Ability
question: Which revision is most appropriate for formal writing?

choices.text: Due to weather being super bad, the activity got moved.
The agency postponed the activity because of severe weather.
The activity was, like, postponed by the agency.
Bad weather kinda made the agency postpone it.

explanation: Formal register is a set of habits, not a matter of long words. Official writing names the actor, uses precise vocabulary, states the cause plainly, and avoids intensifiers, hedges, and fillers borrowed from speech. Option B does all four: the agency acts, 'postponed' is the exact verb, 'severe weather' is the technical description used in advisories, and 'because of' states the reason without padding. Reading the other three aloud reveals the markers that disqualify them — 'super,' 'got,' 'like,' and 'kinda' all belong to casual conversation and would never survive a memorandum.

distractorExplanations.A: 'Super bad' is a conversational intensifier and 'got moved' is a colloquial passive. Both weaken a sentence that should name the agency and state the cause precisely.
distractorExplanations.C: 'Like' is a spoken filler with no grammatical role. The passive also hides nothing useful here, since the agency is named anyway and could simply act as the subject.
distractorExplanations.D: 'Kinda' hedges a fact that is not in doubt, and 'bad weather' is vaguer than the standard term. Formal writing states causes without softening them.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Scan for spoken markers first — super, kinda, sort of, like, got, stuff, a lot of. One of them is enough to disqualify an option on any formal-register item.

subject: Verbal Ability
question: Choose the sentence that clearly expresses cause and effect.

choices.text: Because heavy rain flooded the road, the examination was postponed.
Although it rained, the examination continued.
If it rains, bring an umbrella.
The applicant went to the office to obtain a permit.

explanation: Connectors sort into families, and each family answers a different question. Cause and effect answers 'why did this happen?' and uses because, since, as, so, therefore, and consequently. Option A supplies a genuine cause, flooded roads, and its genuine result, a postponed examination. The other three sentences are all grammatical, but each belongs to a different family: concession admits something that might have prevented the outcome, condition sets a circumstance that has not yet occurred, and purpose names an intended goal. Identifying the family before comparing options makes this item type nearly automatic.

distractorExplanations.B: 'Although' signals concession. It concedes an obstacle and then reports that the outcome happened anyway, which is the reverse of a cause producing an effect.
distractorExplanations.C: 'If' introduces a condition about something that may or may not occur. No rain has fallen yet, so no cause exists and no effect has been produced.
distractorExplanations.D: The infinitive 'to obtain' expresses purpose — the goal the applicant had in mind. A purpose looks forward to an intended result; a cause looks back at what produced one.

tip.label: Remember
tip.text: Sort connectors into four families: CAUSE (because, since, therefore) - CONCESSION (although, even though) - CONDITION (if, unless) - PURPOSE (to, in order to, so that).

subject: Verbal Ability
question: What does the statement "Speed is not enough when accuracy is sacrificed" imply?

choices.text: Speed is always more important than accuracy.
Efficient service must also be accurate.
Accuracy has no place in public service.

explanation: The whole item turns on the phrase 'not enough.' Saying something is not enough concedes that it counts for something while insisting that it does not suffice on its own. Speed therefore remains desirable; what the statement rejects is speed purchased at the cost of accuracy. The implication is that both qualities are required together, which option B states. The trap is a familiar one in reasoning items: readers convert 'insufficient' into 'worthless' and then pick the option that dismisses speed entirely. Keep the two ideas apart — 'not enough' subtracts sufficiency, never value.

distractorExplanations.A: Ranking speed above accuracy is the position the statement argues against. 'Not enough' downgrades speed's standing on its own; it does not elevate speed over anything.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the sentence completely. Accuracy is the quality being defended, and the whole clause exists to insist that it must not be sacrificed.
distractorExplanations.D: Claiming fast service must be inaccurate overshoots. The statement warns about a trade-off that can happen, not one that always happens; speed and accuracy can coexist.

tip.label: Logic Rule
tip.text: 'Not enough' means necessary but insufficient. It never means worthless. Options that erase the first quality entirely have overshot the claim and can be eliminated.

subject: Verbal Ability
question:
Which statement best completes the paragraph?

"Reliable public data helps citizens understand government programs. It also allows researchers to evaluate outcomes. ___"

choices.text: Nevertheless, all records should always remain secret.
For example, inaccurate data improves accountability.
Therefore, agencies should publish accurate data in accessible formats.
In contrast, citizens should avoid official information.

explanation: Read the shape of the paragraph before reading the options. Two sentences list benefits of reliable public data, and the second is linked to the first by 'also,' confirming that the ideas accumulate rather than compete. A closer must therefore draw the consequence of an accumulated case, and the transition that does that is 'Therefore.' Option C also matches in content, converting the two benefits into a recommendation that agencies publish accurately and accessibly. The transition word is the fastest filter available: a contrast signal placed after two agreeing sentences announces an argument that never happened.
steps: Step 1 — Identify the pattern. Both sentences state benefits of reliable public data, and 'also' in the second marks addition, not contrast.
Step 2 — Decide what the closer must do. A list of agreeing benefits calls for a conclusion drawn from them, so the transition needed is one of result.
Step 3 — Filter by transition word. 'Nevertheless' and 'In contrast' both signal opposition, and 'For example' promises an illustration rather than a conclusion.
Step 4 — Check the surviving option for content. 'Therefore, agencies should publish accurate data in accessible formats' follows directly from the two stated benefits.
Step 5 — Option C is the concluding sentence.

distractorExplanations.A: 'Nevertheless' sets up an objection the paragraph never raised, and secrecy contradicts the benefits just described. The absolute 'always' compounds the mismatch.
distractorExplanations.B: 'For example' promises an illustration of the preceding point, yet the sentence delivers the opposite claim: inaccurate data undermines accountability rather than improving it.
distractorExplanations.D: 'In contrast' signals opposition where the paragraph has been building agreement, and advising citizens to avoid official information reverses the paragraph's first benefit.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Filter conclusion items by transition word before reading content. Agreeing sentences take a result signal (therefore, thus, consequently); only a shift in direction earns however or in contrast.
